title: Soil and Water Conservation
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: Soil conservation is the control of soil erosion in order to maintain agricultural productivity.

sections.heading: Causes of Soil Erosion
sections.content: Soil erosion is often the effect of many natural causes, such as water and wind. There are also human factors which increase the rate of soil erosion such as construction, cultivation and other activities.

sections.heading: Why Soil Conservation?
sections.content: Conservation is not just the responsibility of soil and plant scientists, hydrologists, wildlife managers, landowners, and the forest or mine owner alone. All citizens should be made aware about the importance of natural resources as our lives depend on that and everyone should be involved in the process of caring of these resources properly and using them intelligently.

title: Importance of Soil Conservation
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: Soil conservation is crucial in India due to the large area subjected to soil degradation, which threatens the country's food security.

sections.heading: Causes of Soil Degradation
sections.content: India loses about 150 M-ha to water or wind erosion, and an additional 4 M-ha through ravines and gullies. This accounts for 53.3% of the country's total geographical area.

sections.heading: Effects of Soil Degradation
sections.content: Soil degradation threatens India's food security, with a projected population of two billion by 2100 and stagnant food grain production at 211 million tons for the last five years.

sections.heading: Strategies for Soil Conservation
items: Maintain vegetation cover in vulnerable areas to prevent erosion.
Use partial harvesting forests and seasonally dry or wet areas for pasture instead of arable land.
Implement crop rotation to prevent soil exhaustion.
Use contour ploughing in vulnerable areas.
Carefully manage irrigation to reduce soil salinity development.
Manage livestock grazing to prevent overgrazing.
Restrict construction and urbanization to lower agricultural potential areas.
Secure pledges to restore land to its former condition before granting permission for extractive industries.

title: Causes of Soil Degradation
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: Soil degradation may result from natural causes and human-induced causes.

sections.heading: Natural Causes
sections.content: Topographic and climatic factors such as steep slopes, frequent floods and tornadoes, storms and high-velocity wind, high-intensity rains, leaching in humid regions, and drought in dry regions are among the natural causes.

sections.heading: Anthropogenic Causes
sections.content: Deforestation and overexploitation of vegetation, shifting cultivation, soil desurfacing, overgrazing, indiscriminate use of agrochemicals and lack of soil conservation practices, and overextraction of ground water are some anthropogenic causes of soil degradation.

sections.heading: Main Causes of Human-Induced Soil Degradation

title: Deforestation
category: Sustainability and Environment
definition: The conversion of a forest into a non-forest use such as farmland, ranches, pasture, industrial complexes, and urban areas.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.content: Deforestation is expanding and accelerating into the remaining areas of undisturbed forest, and the quality of the remaining forests is declining. Deforestation processes include industrial logging, clear felling, indiscriminate cutting, forest fires, shifting cultivation, and encroachment.

sections.heading: Environmental Impacts
sections.content: The effects of deforestation are loss of forest, loss of biodiversity, climate change, and natural disasters such as cyclones, flood and drought, disruption of water cycle, decline in water quality, soil erosion, and sedimentation.

sections.heading: Consequences for Soil
sections.content: Cutting trees in large tracts results in the climate getting drier in that area. Forest clearance exposes the bare soil to the scorching effect of the sun and the beating action of the rains. Significant amount of top soil is lost by erosion.

sections.heading: Consequences for Climate
sections.content: Deforestation increases the carbon dioxide emission into the atmosphere. Tropical forests account for about 20 % of total global carbon dioxide (CO) emissions

title: Shifting Cultivation
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: Shifting cultivation or slash-and-burn agriculture is an ancient farming system usually practiced by the indigenous people in the hilly areas of the humid tropics.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Shifting Cultivation
sections.content: In this system, a patch of forest, usually on gentle slopes or on summits of hills, is cleared, vegetation is slashed and burned, holes are dug in soil with elementary tools, and seeds of assorted crops are sown before monsoon. Seeds germinate and grow rainfed, and the crops are harvested after 6–8 months. Then the land is left fallow. Farmers clear a new patch of forest for cultivation in the next season.

sections.heading: Effects on Soil and Water
sections.content: The effect of burning is, however, temporary. Rains following burning remove bases rapidly by erosion and leaching. Growing evidence suggests that shifting cultivation in its distorted form leads to an adverse effect on soil and water.

sections.heading: Changes in Rotation Period
items: Settlement of plain landers to hills
Scarcity of available land for cropping

title: Overgrazing
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: Overgrazing is a major cause of soil degradation worldwide.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.content: Livestock are the main source of income in many arid and semiarid countries. Domestic stocks are widely diverse and consist of camels, donkeys, horses, cows, sheep, and goat.

sections.heading: Consequences of Overgrazing
sections.content: The forage and overgrazing of livestock cause a chain of degradation, critically reducing vegetation cover and soil fertility, as well as increasing erosion.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Erosion
items: Domestic animals rapidly clear vegetation, placing stress on a land that already has a low vegetation cover.
They also move in large groups and have sharp hooves that easily break up the soil, leaving it susceptible to erosion.

sections.heading: Impact on Soil Fertility
sections.content: Erosion decreases fertile organic content of the soil. The lack of organic matter can lead to desertification through reduced nutrient availability for plant growth.

title: Soil Desurfacing
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Soil desurfacing refers to the removal of a layer of surface soil for many different purposes, including construction of road and railroads and making of bricks.

sections.heading: Importance of Surface Soil
sections.content: The surface soil is the most fertile part of the soil; it contains the highest organic matter and nutrients and possesses the most suitable physical and chemical conditions for plant growth.

sections.heading: Effects of Soil Desurfacing
items: significantly reduces soil quality and crop yields

title: Monocropping
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: The practice of growing a single crop year after year on the same land, in the absence of rotation through other crops.

sections.heading: Effects on Soil Fertility
sections.content: The roots of the crop draw the same kind and proportion of nutrients from the soil for a long period of time. The nutrient status of the soil becomes imbalanced after a prolonged period of cropping.

sections.heading: Impact on Ecosystems
sections.content: Particular types of insects and pests proliferate. Farmers become increasingly dependent on pesticides.

title: Mismanagement of Irrigation
category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
definition: Irrigation in arid lands can further enhance desertification through salinization and alkalinization.

sections.heading: Causes of Mismanagement of Irrigation
sections.content: It is not possible for farming to occur without artificial irrigation in arid lands where there is a deficiency of moisture. However, irrigation in arid lands can further enhance desertification through salinization and alkalinization.

sections.heading: Effects of Mismanagement of Irrigation
sections.content: Salinization occurs when irrigation water evaporates quickly, leaving natural salts at the surface of the soil. Over a long time, excessive quantities of salts accumulate at or near the soil surface, making it increasingly difficult for plants to extract water from the soil.

sections.heading: Importance of Leaching Requirement
sections.content: Irrigation water must consider the leaching requirement (extra water to leach the salts) of the soil.

title: Use of Heavy Farm Machineries
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Heavy farm machineries are used in mechanized agriculture by developed countries.

sections.heading: Impact on Soil Degradation
sections.content: The impact of heavy farm machineries on soil degradation is discussed in more detail in connection with soil compaction.

title: Soil Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Soil erosion is the detachment and transportation of soil material from one place to another through the action of wind, water in motion or by the beating action of rain drops.

sections.heading: Factors Influencing Soil Erosion
items: Energy group: potential ability of rainfall, runoff and wind to cause erosion (termed erosivity)
Resistance group: erodibility of the soil, depending on its mechanical and chemical properties
Protection group: plant cover, intercepting rainfall and reducing velocity of runoff and wind

sections.heading: Rate of Soil Loss
sections.content: The rate of soil loss is normally expressed in units of mass or volume per unit area per unit of time. Under natural conditions, annual rates are of the order of 0.0045 t ha for areas of moderate relief and 0.45 t ha for steep relief.

sections.heading: Impacts of Soil Erosion
sections.content: Excessive or enhanced soil erosion due to poor land management can result in both on-site and off-site impacts that are detrimental to a whole range of receptors. Where soil erosion occurs, the soil resource can be severely depleted if the rate of erosion exceeds the rate of natural soil formation.

title: Agents of Soil Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Soil erosion is the removal of soil from the land's surface by natural forces such as water, wind, or ice.

sections.heading: Agents of Soil Erosion
sections.content: Water erosion is the removal of soil from the land's surface by running water, including runoff from melted snow and ice. Sheet erosion occurs when thin layers of soil are removed from sloping land due to overland flows. Rill and gully erosion occur when water removes soil from small channels or streams.

sections.heading: Types of Wind Erosion
items: Saltation: Soil particles are carried away by wind in the form of small leaps.
Suspension: Smallest soil particles are thrown into the air and transported by wind to long distances.
Surface creep: Heavier soil particles are pushed or spread along the surface by wind.

sections.heading: Gully Erosion
rows: Gully erosion is an advanced stage of sheet erosion.
The rate of gully erosion depends on various factors such as runoff producing characteristics, drainage area, soil characteristics, and alignment.

title: Landslides or Slip Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The hydraulic pressure caused by heavy rains increases the weight of the rocks at cliffs, which come under the gravitational force and finally slip or fall off.

sections.heading: Landslides
sections.content: Sometimes entire hillock may slide down. In this type of erosion, water and gravity act together.

sections.heading: Stream Bank Erosion
items: The rivers during floods splash their water against the banks and thus cuts through them.
Particularly at curves, water strikes with great speed and the bank caves in alongside.

Weak aggregates are broken apart first.

title: Water Erosion Processes
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The three main processes of water erosion are detachment, transport, and deposition.

sections.heading: Detachment
sections.content: Soil detachment occurs after the soil adsorbs raindrops and pores are filled with water. Raindrops loosen up and break down aggregates. Weak aggregates are broken apart first. Detached fine particles move easily with surface runoff. When dry, detached soil particles form crusts of low permeability.

sections.heading: Transport
sections.content: Detached soil particles are transported in runoff. Smaller particles (e.g., clay) are more readily removed than larger (e.g., sand) particles. The systematic removal of fine particles leaves coarser particles behind. The selective removal modifies the textural and structural properties of the original soil.

sections.heading: Deposition
sections.content: Transported particles deposit in low landscape positions. Most of the eroded soil material is deposited at the downslope end of the fields. Placing the deposited material back to its origin can be costly. Runoff sediment transported off-site can reach downstream water bodies and cause pollution.

title: Sheet Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
definition: Sheet erosion is the removal of a thin layer of soil from the whole slope, primarily by raindrop impact and shallow surface flow.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.content: Soil particles are detached primarily by raindrops and secondarily by frost, hooves of farm animals, tillage, and mechanical action of farm machines. Detached particles are transported by runoff water as overland flow.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Processes
rows: Intensity of accumulation of runoff water depends on the height of the water stream, the coarseness of the surface, vegetation, or crop distribution.

title: Rill Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
definition: Rill erosion occurs when rainfall exceeds the rate of infiltration, causing water to accumulate on the surface and move along sloping lands, concentrating in tiny channels called rills.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.content: Rill erosion is caused by large amounts of material released and transported for variable distances in concentrated areas. It can lead to high soil loss, but the small channels do not usually interfere with tillage implements.

sections.heading: Formation and Characteristics
sections.content: Rills are less than 30 cm deep and are formed by the cutting action of flowing water detaching soil particles. The amount of soil loss may be high, but the small channels do not usually interfere with tillage implements.

sections.heading: Factors Influencing Rill Erosion
items: Tillage lines, rows of crops, and exposed roots

sections.heading: Types of Rill Erosion
rows: Ridge formation with sharply cut rillets and gullies
Material of varying resistance, vertical openings

title: Gully Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The main feature of gully erosion is the volume and velocity of water at the lowest level.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Gullies
sections.content: Gullies may grow into gorges and canyons in high altitudes and very steep slopes. Gullies may be flat, narrow, broad, and round.

sections.heading: Types of Gully Forms
items: Flat forms occur mostly on shallow soil or in connection with a specific lithic structure of the slope.
Narrow, acute forms are created with a narrow V-section, the breadth of the gully usually being equal to its depth or smaller.
Broad gullies have a wide bottom and are U shaped.

sections.heading: Active Gullies
sections.content: Active gullies maintain steep or even perpendicular sides. It happens frequently that recent forms replace older forms so that their origin and age cannot be assessed from superficial observation.

title: Riverbank/Stream Bank Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The process of erosion that occurs along the banks of rivers and streams, characterized by the formation of gullies, canyons, and other landforms.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Gully Erosion
sections.content: Gullies may grow into gorges and canyons in high altitudes and very steep slopes. Gullies may be flat, narrow, broad, and round.

sections.heading: Types of Gullies
items: Flat forms occur mostly on shallow soil or in connection with a specific lithic structure of the slope.
Narrow, acute forms are created with a narrow V-section, the breadth of the gully usually being equal to its depth or smaller.
Broad gullies have a wide bottom and are U shaped.

sections.heading: Factors Influencing Gully Erosion
sections.content: The main feature of gully erosion is the volume and velocity of water at the lowest level. The energy of flowing water increases its cutting and smashing power and often results in bank erosion.

title: Gully Erosion
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
definition: A channel or miniature valley cut by concentrated runoff through which water commonly flows only during and immediately after heavy rains.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Gully Erosion
sections.content: Any concentration of surface runoff is a potential source of gully erosion. A gully is too large to be filled by normal tillage practices.

sections.heading: Distinction between Ravine, Gully and Rills
sections.content: A gully is too large to be filled by normal tillage practices. A ravine is a deep narrow gorge.

title: Development of Gullies
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The main processes in the development of gullies are waterfall erosion and channel erosion.

sections.heading: Process of Development
sections.content: Gullies usually start with channel erosion. When an overfall develops at the head of the gully, the gully continues to develop by waterfall erosion.

sections.heading: Types of Erosion
items: Waterfall erosion extends the gully head
Channel erosion enlarges the depth and width of gullies

title: Principles of Gully Control
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Minimizing surface runoff is essential in gully control.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Gully Erosion
sections.content: The rate of gully erosion depends primarily on the runoff producing characteristics of the watershed, the watershed area, soil characteristics, size-shape and slope of gully etc.

sections.heading: Methods for Gully Control
items: Improvement of gully catchments to reduce and regulate the runoff rates (peak flows)
Diversion of surface water above the gully area
Stabilization of gullies by structural measures and accompanying re-vegetation

title: Gully Control Measures

definition: Preventing the formation of gully is much easier than controlling it once it has formed.

sections.heading: Planning for Gully Control
sections.content: One of the major steps in a gully control programme is to plan the control of runoff from the drainage area. The various methods employed for controlling runoff may be considered in the following order:

title: Retention of Runoff on the Drainage Area
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Retention of runoff on the drainage area can be achieved through good crop management and applicable conservation practices.

sections.heading: Methods for Reducing Runoff
sections.content: crop management and applicable conservation practices such as contouring, strip cropping, bunding, terracing etc. Where contour bunds are used, runoff is greatly reduced. On cultivated areas, small and medium sized gullies can also be reclaimed by placing a series of earthfills across the gully.

title: Diversion of Runoff Around the Gullied Area: The most effective

definition: control of gullies is by complete elimination of runoff from the gullied area.

sections.heading: Methods for Diverting Runoff
sections.content: Terraces and diversion ditches are generally used for diverting runoff from its natural outlet.

sections.heading: Use of Terraces
sections.content: Terraces are very effective in the control of small gullies on cultivated fields or even medium size shallow gullies.

sections.heading: Alternative Methods for Diversion Ditches
sections.content: If the slope above a gully is too steep for terracing, or if the drainage area is pasture or woodland, diversion ditches may be used to keep the runoff out of the gully.

sections.heading: Conveyance of Runoff through the Gully
sections.content: If it is not possible to either retain or divert the runoff, then runoff must be conveyed through the gully itself.

title: Sod Flumes
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A sod flume is a type of structure used to control overfall in gullies, providing a protected surface for runoff to flow into the gully.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.content: The design of sod flume serves the purpose of preventing further waterfall erosion by providing a protected surface over which the runoff may flow into the gully. Slope varies with the soil type, size of watershed, height of overfall and type of sod used.

sections.heading: Design Parameters
items: Slope: varies with soil type, watershed size, overfall height, and sod type.

sections.heading: Design Guidelines
sections.content: The flume should be wide enough to maintain a non-erosive velocity. A slope of 4:1 is considered the steepest for its design.

title: Temporary Gully Control Structures (TGCS)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: TGCS have a life span of 3 to 8 years and they are pretty effective where the amount of runoff is not too large.

sections.heading: Purpose and Function
sections.content: These are made of locally available materials. Basic purposes they serve are to retain more water as well as soil for proper plant growth and prevent channel erosion until sufficient vegetation is established on the upstream side of the gully.

title: Design Criteria for Temporary Check Dams
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The overall height of a temporary check dam should not exceed 75 cm, with an effective height of about 30 cm being sufficient.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.content: Life of the check dams under ordinary conditions should be in between 3 to 8 years. Spillway capacity of check dams is generally designed to handle peak runoff that may be expected once in 5 to 10 year return period.

sections.heading: Spacing and Apron
sections.content: Check dams should be spaced so that the crest elevation of one dam is at the same level as the bottom elevation of the adjacent dam upstream. An apron or platform must be provided at the down-stream end to catch water falling over the top.

title: General
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Used in gullies of moderate slopes (not more than 10 percent) and small drainage areas that do not have flood flows which carry rocks and boulders. Help in the establishment of vegetation for permanent control of erosion.

sections.heading: Dam Construction
sections.content: Dam is built in half-moon shape with the open end up- stream.

sections.heading: Optimum Curvature
items: The amount of curvature is arbitrary: but an off-set equal to 1/6 of the width of gully at the dam site is optimum.

title: Construction
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A row of posts is set along the curve of a proposed dam at about 1.2 m intervals and 60-90 cm deep.

sections.heading: Setting up the Dam
sections.content: To construct a woven-wire dam, a row of posts is set along the curve of the proposed dam at about 1.2 m intervals and 60-90 cm deep. Heavy gauge woven wire is placed against the post with the lower part set in a trench (15-20 cm deep), and 25-30 cm projected above the ground surface along the spillway width. Rock, brush or sod may be placed approximately up to a length of 1.2 m to form the apron. For sealing the structure, straw, fine brush or similar material should be placed against the wire on the upstream side upto the height of spillway.

title: Construction
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
definition: A structure, such as a dam, is constructed by covering the sides and bottom of a gully with straw or fine mulch, followed by the placement of stakes and brushes to hold it in place.

sections.heading: Construction Process
sections.content: For a distance of 3-4.5 m along the site of the structure, sides and bottom of the gully are covered with thin layer of straw or similar fine mulch. Brushes are then packed closely together over the mulch to about one half of the proposed height of dam.

sections.heading: Stake Placement
items: Several rows of stakes are driven crosswise in the gully, with rows 60 cm apart, and stakes 30-60 cm apart in the rows.
Heavy galvanized wire is used to fasten the stakes in a row, as well as to firmly compress the brushes in places.

sections.heading: Additional Support
sections.content: Sometimes large stones are also placed on top of brush to keep it compressed and in close contact with the bottom of the gully.

sections.heading: Maintenance Requirements
sections.content: Major weakness is the difficulty of preventing the leaks and constant attention is required to plug openings of appropriate size with straw as they develop.

sections.heading: Construction

If the rocks are small, they should be enclosed in a cage of woven- wire.

title: The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The most widely used empirical model worldwide for estimating soil loss, developed in the USA.

sections.heading: Limitations of the USLE
sections.content: The USLE makes simplified assumptions in the processes of soil erosion and has limited consideration of complex factors.

sections.heading: Advantages of the USLE
sections.content: The USLE is simple, easy to use, and does not require numerous input parameters or extensive data sets for prediction.

sections.heading: Equation Components
items: R: rainfall and runoff erosivity index

sections.heading: Equation Formula
sections.content: A = R*K*LS*C*P, where A is average annual soil loss (Mg ha)

title: Rainfall and Runoff Erosivity Index (EI)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The EI is computed as the product of total storm energy times the intensity of the rain.

sections.heading: Computing the EI
sections.content: The USLE uses the annual EI which is computed by adding the EI values from individual storms that occurred during the year.

sections.heading: Relationship to Soil Loss
sections.content: According to Wischmeier and Smith (1978), the EI corresponds closely to the amount of soil loss from a field.

sections.heading: Limitations of the USLE-Computed EI
sections.content: The USLE-computed EI is only valid for rain intensities ≤ 63.5mm h.

sections.heading: Modifications for Tropical Regions

sections.heading: EI Values and Region Type

Values of EI above 500 (mm h) correspond to humid regions.

title: Limitations of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The USLE model applies only to sheet erosion since it is based on rain as a source of energy, making it unsuitable for linear or mass erosion.

sections.heading: Applicability Limitations
sections.content: The USLE model has been tested and verified in plain and hilly countries with 1-20% slopes, but excludes young mountains with steeper than 40% slopes.

sections.heading: Regional Limitations
items: only applicable to the American Great Plains

sections.heading: Temporal Limitations
sections.content: The model applies only for average data over 20 years and is not valid for individual storms.

sections.heading: Methodological Limitations
sections.content: The USLE neglects certain interactions between factors to distinguish the individual effect of each factor, such as slope combined with plant cover or soil type along with slope.

sections.heading: Omission of Sediment Deposition
sections.content: The USLE does not calculate sediment deposition.

title: Soil Loss Measurement Techniques
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Data on soil erosion and its controlling factors can be collected in the field or, for simulated conditions, in the laboratory.

sections.heading: Advantages of Field Measurements
sections.content: For realistic data on soil loss, field measurements are the most reliable, but because conditions vary in both time and space, it is often difficult to determine the chief causes of erosion or to understand the processes at work.

sections.heading: Limitations of Field Measurements
sections.content: Because conditions vary in both time and space, it is often difficult to determine the chief causes of erosion or to understand the processes at work.

sections.heading: Advantages of Laboratory Experiments
sections.content: Experiments designed to lead to explanation are best undertaken in the laboratory, where the effects of many factors can be controlled.

sections.heading: Need for Field Verification
sections.content: Because of the artificiality of laboratory experiments, however, some confirmation of their results in the field is desirable.

title: Experimental Design
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The process of planning, conducting, and analyzing experiments to assess the influence of one or more factors on a specific outcome.

sections.heading: Designing Experiments
sections.content: Experiments are usually carried out to assess the influence of one or more factors on the rate of erosion. In a simple experiment to study the effect of slope steepness, it is assumed that all other factors likely to influence erosion are held constant.

sections.heading: Factors to Consider
items: levels for factors being held constant

sections.heading: Experimental Error and Variability
sections.content: Measurements are subject to error. Since no single measurement of soil loss can be considered as the absolutely correct value, it is virtually impossible to quantify errors.However; they can be assessed in respect of variability.

sections.heading: Experimental Design Considerations
sections.content: A decision is also needed on what levels to set for the factors being held constant, e.g. whether slope length should be 5 or 50m, or the rainfall intensity 20 or 200mmh-1.

sections.heading: Data Collection and Analysis
sections.content: A problem faced in many experiments is how much data to collect. For instance, if the objective of a study is to measure total soil loss over a period of time, this can be achieved by collecting in bulk all the soil washed or blown from an area.

sections.heading: Best Practices for Experimental Design
sections.content: Experiments should have clearly conceived objectives, define what needs to be measured and at what level of accuracy, and be set up in such a way that they can be easily repeated by others.

definition: Field measurements may be classified into two groups: those designed to determine soil loss from relatively small sample areas or erosion plots, often as part of an experiment, and those designed to assess erosion over a larger area, such as a drainage basin.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content: Field measurements may be classified into two groups:

title: Erosion Plots: Bounded Plots
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Bounded plots are physically isolated pieces of land used to study erosion, with both runoff and soil loss monitored.

sections.heading: Design and Construction
sections.content: Plots are made of stable materials like sheet metal, wood, or other non-rotting materials. Edges extend 150–200mm above the soil surface and are embedded in the soil to prevent shifting.

sections.heading: Layout and Data Collection
sections.content: A collecting trough or gutter channels sediment and runoff into tanks, with an overflow system for large plots. However, this setup has several sources of error, including silting and inadequate covering against rainfall.

sections.heading: Considerations and Limitations
items: Collecting tanks overflowing during extreme events
Tanks floating out of saturated ground
Runoff entering the top of the plots
Damage from termites, spiders, and baboons

title: Gerlach Troughs
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
definition: An alternative method of measuring sediment loss and runoff using simple metal gutters, closed at the sides and fitted with a movable lid.

sections.heading: Design and Layout
sections.content: Two or three gutters are placed side-by-side across the slope and groups of gutters are installed at different slope lengths, arranged in plan to ensure a clear run to each gutter from en echelon the slope crest.

sections.heading: Calculating Soil Loss
items: Soil loss per unit width is normal.
If an areal assessment is required, assume a catchment area equal to the width of the gutter times the length of the slope.

sections.heading: Advantages and Limitations
sections.content: Gerlach troughs can be employed for sample measurements of soil loss at a large number of selected sites over a large area due to their cheapness and simplicity. However, on curved slopes, the catchment area must be surveyed in the field.

title: Changes in Ground Level
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The simplest way of measuring changes in ground level over time is to use an erosion pin, a 250–300 mm long nail driven through a washer into the soil.

sections.heading: Installation and Measurement
sections.content: A large number of pins, usually installed on a grid system, is needed to obtain representative data over a large area. A disadvantage of erosion pins is that they can be easily disturbed by livestock and wildlife or stolen by the local population.

sections.heading: Alternative Approach
sections.content: An alternative approach is to establish a network of metal pegs, set unobtrusively in concrete at ground level so that their position remains stable over time. The method, pioneered by Hudson (1964) on rangeland in Zimbabwe, is known as the erosion bridge.

sections.heading: Erosion Bridge Method
sections.content: A portable aluminium girder is placed across any two adjacent pegs from which vertical readings of the depth to the soil surface can be taken at regular intervals. Between readings the girder is removed.

title: Splash Erosion Measurements
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Erosion measurements in the field using splash boards, small funnels or bottles to collect splashed material.

sections.heading: Methods of measuring splash erosion
sections.content: Erosion plots, Gerlach troughs, erosion pins and erosion bridges provide information on erosion by rainsplash, overland flow and rills combined. Attempts to assess the relative contributions of each are based on separate measurements of splash erosion and rill erosion with the balance being attributed to overland flow.

sections.heading: Alternative approach
sections.content: The field splash cup method, where a block of soil is isolated by enclosing it in a central cylinder and the material splashed out is collected in a surrounding catching tray.

title: Rill Erosion Measurement
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The simplest method of assessing rill erosion is to establish a series of transects, 20–100 m long, across the slope and positioned one above the other.

sections.heading: Method
sections.content: Establish a series of transects, 20–100 m long, across the slope and positioned one above the other.

title: Gully Erosion Measurement
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Rates of gully erosion are calculated from differences in elevation between DEMs of different dates.

sections.heading: Measurement Techniques
sections.content: Erosion from relatively small gullies can be assessed using the same profiling technique as described above for rills. For larger gullies, sequential surveys using aerial photography are more suitable.

sections.heading: Aerial Photography Surveys
items: More recent surveys of gullies use large-scale (1 : 10,000) aerial photography to construct high resolution digital elevation models (DEMs). Digitally generated DEMs can match the accuracy of traditional analytical photogrammetric techniques and are much faster to produce.

title: Catchments Sediment Yield
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The sediment yield of a catchment is obtained from measurements of the quantity of sediment leaving a catchment along the river over time.

sections.heading: Measurement Methods
sections.content: Recording stations are established at the exit point for the automatic measurement of discharge, using weirs and depth recorders, and suspended sediment concentrations in the river water. Water samples are taken at set times with specially designed integrated sediment samplers, or the sediment concentration is monitored continuously by recording the turbidity of the water.

sections.heading: Limitations of Measurement Methods
sections.content: Bucket samples are not recommended because they contain only the surface water and cannot provide information on the sediment being transported throughout the depth and width of the river channel. With measurements made at set times, there is a need to extrapolate the data to cover the period between samples.

sections.heading: Sediment Discharge Rating Curve
sections.content: The standard approach is to establish a sediment discharge rating curve in which the sediment concentration (C) is related to the water discharge () by the equation C =aQ(6.2).

sections.heading: Accuracy and Sampling Frequency
sections.content: The accuracy of this method is highly dependent on the frequency of sampling. The likelihood of underestimation increased as the sampling frequency decreased, since, with longer sampling intervals, the record is likely to include fewer flood events.

sections.heading: Turbidity Meter Limitations
sections.content: The turbidity meter does not give a true record because the measurements are subject to errors associated with the influence of the particle size of the sediment load, the magnitude of the sediment concentration, the presence of organic matter and the need to keep the sensors clear of algae.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.content: Despite these problems, the method is currently the best available to provide estimates of suspended sediment yield, especially if high frequency data are needed. It should be recognized, however that, because of the need for regular calibration and maintenance, such data come at greater cost compared to using rating curves.

title: Reservoir Surveys
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: A method used to measure the amount of sediment accumulated in a reservoir, which can indicate erosion rates in the catchment upstream.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.content: Reservoir surveys involve measuring the depth of the reservoir using manual soundings or echo-sounders, and creating a contour map of the bottom. The volume of sediment is then calculated and compared to the initial volume to determine erosion rates.

sections.heading: Calculations
items: Volume below lowest contour: product of area of lowest contour and mean depth from bottom

sections.heading: Data Analysis
sections.content: The volume is converted into mass, divided by the catchment area to give an erosion value in t ha, which is then adjusted for sediment representation and time since reservoir construction.

title: Tracers
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A tracer is a substance used to measure or study a process, often in environmental science or agriculture.

sections.heading: Caesium-137 Tracer
sections.content: Caesium-137 is the most commonly used tracer in soil erosion measurement. It was produced in the fall-out of atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons from the 1950s to 1970s.

sections.heading: Laboratory Experiments
sections.content: Laboratory experiments are used to study soil erosion and deposition, but they have limitations due to scale-equivalence issues.

sections.heading: Rainfall Simulation
rows: Hypodermic needles or capillary tubes and nozzles

title: Runoff Simulation
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: A setup used in experimental geomorphology to simulate runoff, often using a flume with adjustable slope and controlled discharge.

sections.heading: Setup and Design
sections.content: The Experimental Geomorphology Laboratory at the University of Leuven uses an aluminium and plexiglass flume to simulate runoff. The flume is 4m long and 0.4m wide, with a controlled discharge from a cylinder with ten openings.

sections.heading: Adjusting Slope and Discharge
sections.content: The slope of the flume can be adjusted to different steepnesses, and rainfall simulators positioned over the top. The discharge is controlled by a tap, with water pumped from a container at the upper end.

sections.heading: Reducing Edge Effects
sections.content: To reduce edge effects, sediment can be collected from a narrow strip down the centre of the plot instead of collecting for the whole plot width. This helps to eliminate the problem of difficult-to-eliminate edge effects.

sections.heading: Simulating Rill Erosion
sections.content: The short length of the flume makes it difficult to simulate rill erosion, but the supply of runoff at the top of the slope can be adjusted to simulate different slope lengths.

sections.heading: Adding Sediment
sections.content: Sediment can also be added to the runoff upslope of the test soil to further simulate real-world conditions.

title: Wind Tunnels
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: A laboratory facility used to study wind erosion, where air is supplied by a fan through a honeycomb shield into a convergence zone, test section, and divergence zone.

sections.heading: Design of Wind Tunnels
sections.content: Wind tunnels are shaped so that air enters through a honeycomb shield, serving as a flow straightener, into a convergence zone, where flow is constricted, passes through the test section and leaves through a divergence zone.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Closed-Circuit Tunnels
rows: Easier due to less upstream contact with boundary walls

title: Principles of Erosion Control
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Soil erosion takes place both due to natural causes and anthropogenic factors, with adverse effects including loss of valuable top soil, sedimentation in rivers and irrigation canals, and structural damages.

sections.heading: Erosion Control Measures
sections.content: Soil erosion control measures are adopted to reduce or minimize the intensity of the adverse effects. Catchment Area Treatment (CAT) is adopted to reduce soil loss from catchments due to runoff flow, after ascertaining erosion severity on sub-watershed basis.

sections.heading: Catchment Area Treatment (CAT)
sections.content: CAT comprises mechanical (engineering) and vegetative (afforestation) measures. Mechanical and vegetative practices on agricultural lands are employed on the milder slopes for conservation of soil, by farming across the slope of the land.

sections.heading: Principles Underlying Erosion Control
sections.content: The basic principle underlying this approach is to cause reduction in the effect of the runoff velocity and, thereby reduce soil erosion. On steeper slopes, mechanical measures (such as terracing) and other structures are constructed to reduce the effect of the slope on runoff velocity.

title: Contour Bunds
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Contour bunds are a type of bund used to prevent soil erosion, recommended for areas with low annual rainfall, permeable soils, and gentle land slopes.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Uses
sections.content: The choice of bund type depends on land slope, rainfall, soil type, and the purpose of the bund. Contour bunds are suitable for areas with low annual rainfall (< 600 mm), agricultural fields with permeable soils, and gentle land slopes.

sections.heading: Comparison with Graded Bunds
items: Used in areas with high rainfall and relatively impervious soil for safe disposal of excess runoff.
Not suitable for black cotton soils due to severe erosion problems.

sections.heading: Performance in Different Soil Conditions
sections.content: Bunds can stand well in shallow, medium, and medium deep soils. However, they fail in deep black soil due to cracks that allow water to flow through, causing breaches and severe damage to fields.

title: Contour Bunds
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Contour bunds are laid out in areas with less rainfall and permeable soils to prevent soil erosion and conserve rainwater.

sections.heading: Main Functions
items: It reduces the length of slope which in turn reduces the soil erosion.
The water is impounded for some time and gets recharged into the soil which helps in crop cultivation.

sections.heading: Limitations
items: The contour bunds are suitable for those areas, which receive the annual rainfall less than 600 mm
It is not suitable for clayey soils
Contour bunding is not suitable on the land slopes greater than 6%

title: Graded Bunds
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Graded bunds are laid out in areas where the land is susceptible to water erosion, the soil is less permeable and the area has water logging problems.

sections.heading: Design and Construction
sections.content: A graded bund system is designed to dispose of excess runoff safely from agricultural fields. A graded bund is laid out with a longitudinal slope gradient leading to outlet.

sections.heading: Variable-Graded Bunds
sections.content: The variable-graded bunds are required where bunds need longer lengths, owing to which the cumulative runoff increases towards the outlets. In these types of bunds, variations in the grade are provided at different sections of the bund to keep the runoff velocity within the desired limits so as not to cause any soil erosion.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.content: Due to crossing of farm implements, the bunds are disturbed and some soil is lost. Proper maintenance is required at regular interval.

title: Type of Bund
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The type of bund (contour or graded bund) to be constructed depends upon the rainfall and soil condition.

sections.heading: Construction Considerations
sections.content: Contour bunds are preferred for construction in areas receiving annual rainfall less than 600 mm and where soil moisture is a limiting factor for crop production. Graded bunds are recommended in heavy and medium rainfall areas.

title: Spacing of the Bunds
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The spacing of bunds should meet specific criteria to ensure optimal water management.

sections.heading: Principles for Spacing of Bunds
sections.content: The seepage zone below the upper bund should meet the saturation zone of the lower bund; the bunds should check the water at a point where the water attains erosive velocity; and the bund should not cause inconvenience to agricultural operations.

sections.heading: Formula for Determining Spacing
sections.content: The formula used to determine spacing is: V.I. = vertical interval between consecutive bunds, S = land slope (percent), and a and b are constants depending on soil and rainfall characteristics.

sections.heading: Modified Formula for Heavy Rainfall
sections.content: For areas of heavy rainfall: V.I. = vertical interval in cm, S = land slope in percent

sections.heading: Modified Formula for Low Rainfall
sections.content: For areas with low rainfall: V.I. = vertical interval in cm, S = land slope in percent

title: Definition of Agricultural Finance
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Agricultural finance is the money extended to farmers to stimulate the productivity of limited farm resources.

sections.content: Murray (in 1953) defined agricultural finance as an economic study of borrowing funds by farmers, the organization and operation of farm lending agencies and of society’s interest in credit for agriculture. Tandon and Dhondyal (1962) defined it as a branch of agricultural economics, which deals with financial resources related to individual farm units.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Muniraj (1987) has more specifically defined it as: Farm finance is the money extended to the farmers to stimulate the productivity of limited farm resources. It is not a mere loan or credit of advance, it is and instrument to promote the well-being of the society. It is not just a science to manage the money, but is an applied science of allocating scarce resources to derive the optimum out-put. It is a level with forward & backward linkages to the economic development both at micro & micro level.

title: Nature and Scope
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Agricultural finance can be dealt at both micro level and macro level, with macro finance dealing with the financing of agriculture as a whole in the economy and micro finance referring to financial management of individual farm business units.

sections.heading: Micro- Finance
sections.content: It is concerned with the study as to how the individual farmer considers various sources of credit, quantum of credit to be borrowed from each source and how he allocates the same among the alternative uses within the farm.

sections.heading: Macro- Finance
sections.content: It deals with the aspects relating to total credit needs of the agricultural sector, the terms and conditions under which the credit is available and the method of use of total credit for the development of agriculture.

title: Purpose of Grassed Waterways
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: Grassed waterways are used as outlets to prevent rill and gully formation, while also improving soil aeration and water quality.

sections.heading: Benefits of Grassed Waterways
sections.content: These waterways can reduce sedimentation of nearby water bodies and pollutants in runoff. The vegetation improves the soil aeration and water quality (impacting the aquatic habitat) due to its nutrient removal through plant uptake and sorption by soil.

sections.heading: Wildlife Habitat
sections.content: The waterways can also provide a wildlife habitat.

title: Design of Grassed Waterways
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The designs of grassed waterways are similar to the design of irrigation channels and are designed based on their functional requirements.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.content: Generally, these waterways are designed for carrying the maximum runoff for a 10- year recurrence interval period. The rational formula is invariably used to determine the peak runoff rate. Waterways can be shorter in length or sometimes, can be even very long.

sections.heading: Design Criteria
items: For shorter lengths, the estimated flow at the waterways outlets forms the design criterion.
For longer lengths, a variable capacity waterway is designed to account for the changing drainage areas.

title: Size of Waterway
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The size of the waterway depends upon the expected runoff.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.content: A 10 year recurrence interval is used to calculate the maximum expected runoff to the waterway. As the catchment area of the waterway increases towards the outlet, the expected runoff is calculated for different reaches of the waterway and used for design purposes.

sections.heading: Cross-Sectional Area Calculation
sections.content: The cross-sectional area is calculated using the formula: a = Q/V (9.1) where,  = cross-sectional area of the channel, Q = expected maximum runoff, and  = velocity of flow.

title: Selection of Suitable Grasses
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The selection of suitable grasses for construction of grassed waterways is influenced by various factors including soil and climate conditions, duration of establishment, runoff volume and velocity, ease of establishment, and cost and availability of seeds.

sections.heading: Factors to Consider
items: time required to develop a good vegetative cover
suitability for utilization as feed or hay
redundancy to shallow flows in relation to sedimentation

sections.heading: Preferred Grasses
sections.content: Rhizomatous grasses are preferred for waterways because they spread quickly and provide more protection than brush grasses.

sections.heading: Deep Rooted Legumes
sections.content: Deep rooted legumes are seldom used for grassed waterways due to their tendency to loosen the soil, making it erodible under fast flowing runoff water.

title: Construction Procedure and Maintenance
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The construction of a waterway should be done when the field is in meadow and the amount of runoff from the area is also very less.

sections.heading: Steps for Construction
sections.content: The construction of grassed waterways is carried out using the following steps.

title: Step-1: Shaping (Soil Digging)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The shaping of the waterway should be done as straight and even as possible.

sections.heading: Key Considerations
sections.content: Any sudden fall or sharp turn must be eliminated, except in the area where the structure is planned to be installed in the waterway. In addition, the grade should also be shaped according to the designed plan. Also, the stones and stumps which are likely to interfere with the discharge rate must be removed.

title: Step-2: Grass Planting
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The planting of grasses is very important after shaping the waterway channel, with local species being prioritized.

sections.heading: Importance of Grass Planting
sections.content: Priorities should always be given to the local species of grasses.

sections.heading: Seeding vs Sodding
sections.content: In large waterways, seeding is cheaper than sodding.

title: Ballasting
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Ballasting is done in those localities where rocks are readily available adjacent to the sites and waterway gradient is very steep.

sections.heading: General Recommendations for Ballasting
sections.content: Ballasting is generally recommended for the waterways in the small farms. The stones to be used for this purpose should be at least of 15 to 20 cm diameter; and they should be placed firmly on the ground.

sections.heading: Stability Considerations
sections.content: From stability point of view, on very steep slopes, wire mesh should be used to encase the stones. In parabolic shaped waterways, partial ballasting should be done in the centre, leaving the sides with grass protection.

title: Placing of Structure
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: A constructed structure is essential to handle sudden falls in waterway flow paths, preventing soil scouring.

sections.heading: Importance of Structures
sections.content: Structures are necessary to prevent soil scouring due to falling water flow from higher to lower elevations.

sections.heading: Design and Construction Considerations
items: The structure must be strong enough to handle designed flows.
Water should not flow around the structure but through its top.
The structure should be built on firm soils with a deep foundation.

sections.heading: Apron and Stilling Basin Requirements
sections.content: The apron or stilling basin of drop structures must be strong enough to absorb or dissipate the energy/impact of falling water.

sections.heading: Post-Construction Measures
items: Earth filling should be done around the structure and consolidated properly.
Proper sodding is required at the junction of earth filling and the structure to prevent tunneling.

title: Maintenance
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: The maintenance of waterways is crucial for watershed conservation or land treatment system.

sections.heading: Importance of Maintenance
sections.content: The grasses grown in waterway should always be kept short and flexible, so that they shingle as water flows over them, but do not lodge permanently.

sections.heading: Maintenance Process
items: Grassed waterways should not be used as footpaths, animal tracks, or as grazing grounds.
Frequent crossing of waterways by wheeled vehicles should not be allowed.
Newly established waterways should be kept under strict watch.
Large waterways should be kept under protection with fencing.

sections.heading: Preventive Measures
sections.content: The bushes or large plants grown in the waterway should be removed immediately as they may endanger the growth of grasses. The level of grass in waterway should be kept as low and uniform as possible to avoid turbulent flow.

sections.heading: Tillage Operations
sections.content: Similarly, if waterways are to be crossed by tillage implements, they should be disengaged, plough should be lifted and disc straightened. Tillage operation should also be done following nearly the contour.

sections.heading: Inspection and Repair
sections.content: If there is any damage of the waterway, it should be quickly repaired so that the damage may not enlarge due to rainfalls. Waterways must be inspected frequently during first two rainy seasons, after construction.

title: Types of Water Harvesting

sections.heading: Types of Water Harvesting
sections.content: Three types of water harvesting are covered by rainwater harvesting. Water collected from roof tops, courtyards and similar compacted or treated surfaces is used for domestic purpose or garden crops. Micro-catchment water harvesting is a method of collecting surface runoff from a small catchment area and storing it in the root zone of an adjacent infiltration basin. The basin is planted with a tree, a bush or with annual crops. Macro-catchment water harvesting, also called harvesting from external catchments is the case where runoff from hill-slope catchments is conveyed to the cropping area located at foothill on flat terrain.

title: Short Term Runoff Harvesting Techniques
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Contour Bunds involve constructing bunds on the contour of a catchment area to hold surface runoff.

sections.heading: Construction Details
sections.content: The height of contour bund generally ranges from 0.30 to 1.0 m and length from 10 to a few 100 meters.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.content: The side slope of the bund should be as per the requirement.

title: Semicircular Hoop
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
definition: A semicircular hoop is a type of structure consisting of an earthen impartment constructed in the shape of a semicircle, used for irrigation.

sections.heading: Design and Construction
sections.content: The tips of the semicircular hoop are furnished on the contour. The water contributed from the area is collected within the hoop to a maximum depth equal to the height of the embankment.

sections.heading: Arrangement and Layout
sections.content: The rows of semicircular hoops are arranged in a staggered form so that the over flowing water from the upper row can be easily interrupted by the lower row.

sections.heading: Usage and Applications
sections.content: Such type of structure is mostly used for irrigation of grasses, fodder, shrubs, trees etc.

title: Rock Catchment
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The rock catchments are exposed rock surfaces used for collecting runoff water in a depressed area.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.content: When rainfall occurs on the exposed rock surface, runoff takes place rapidly because there is little loss. The runoff is drained towards the lowest point called the storage tank and the harvested water is stored there.

sections.heading: Design considerations
items: The area of rock catchment may vary from 100 m to few 1000 m; accordingly the dimensions of the storage tank should also be designed.
The water collected in the tank can be used for domestic use or irrigation purposes.

sections.heading: Ground Catchment
sections.content: A large area of ground is used as catchment for runoff yield. The runoff is diverted into a storage tank where it is stored. The ground is cleared from vegetation and compacted very well.

title: Long Term Runoff Harvesting Techniques
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: Long term runoff harvesting is done for building a large water storage for the purpose of irrigation, fish farming, electricity generation etc.

sections.heading: Design Criteria
sections.content: Watershed should contribute a sufficient amount of runoff. There should be suitable collection site, where water can be safely stored. Appropriate techniques should be used for minimizing various types of water losses such as seepage and evaporation during storage and its subsequent use in the watershed. There should also be some suitable methods for efficient utilization of the harvested water for maximizing crop yield per unit volume of available water.

sections.heading: Types of Long Term Runoff Harvesting Structures
Dugout Ponds
sections.content: The dugout ponds are constructed by excavating the soil from the ground surface. These ponds may be fed by ground water or surface runoff or by both. Construction of these ponds is limited to those areas which have land slope less than 4% and where water table lies within 1.5-2 meters depth from the ground surface (Fig. 10.4). Dugout ponds involve more construction cost, therefore these are generally recommended when embankment type ponds are not economically feasible.

sections.heading: Water Harvesting Pond
sections.content: The farm ponds can be considered as water harvesting ponds. They may be dugout or embankment type. Their capacity depends upon the size of catchment area. title: Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme (CCIS)
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
definition: The Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme (CCIS) was introduced by GIC in all the states in 1985, covering farmers who availed crop loans for cereals such as paddy, wheat, millets, oil seeds, and pulses.

sections.heading: Eligibility
sections.content: The scheme covers all farmers who availed the crop loan and is limited to cereals such as paddy, wheat, millets, oil seeds, and pulses.

sections.heading: Insurance Periods
items: Loans given from 1st April to 30th September qualify for kharif insurance business.
Loans granted from 1st October to March 31st of next year qualify for rabi insurance.

sections.heading: Insurance Cover
rows: 100 per cent of crop loan taken by the farmers during that season
Rs. 10,000 /- per farmer for all insurable crops

sections.heading: Premium Calculation
sections.content: The insurance premium is fixed at 2 per cent of sum insured for paddy, wheat, and millets, and 1 per cent for oilseeds and pulses.

sections.heading: Subsidy
items: 50 per cent of insurance premium is subsidized by the central and state governments in equal proportion for small and marginal farmers

sections.heading: Indemnity Calculation
sections.content: The indemnity payable under the scheme is calculated on the basis of "threshold yield" and is equal to 80 per cent of the average yield for a given crop for the previous 5 years.

title: Advantages of CCIS
category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech

sections.heading: Boosting Productivity

sections.heading: Revitalizing High-Risk Areas

which otherwise would have remained uncultivated

title: Demerits of CCIS
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: The scheme provided coverage only to a limited number of crops, excluding important cash crops, and was not effective in agriculturally intensive states.

sections.heading: Coverage Limitations
sections.content: It provided coverage only to a limited number of crops like wheat, paddy, oilseeds, millets and pulses excluding important cash crops like sugarcane, potato, cotton etc.

sections.heading: Geographical Ineffectiveness
sections.content: As the coverage was restricted to rainfed crops only, the scheme was not effective in agriculturally intensive states such as Punjab, Haryana and Western U.P.

sections.heading: Eligibility Restrictions
sections.content: The scheme covered only those farmers who had availed crop loans from financial institutions.

sections.heading: Financial Limitations
sections.content: Sum insured per farmer was also limited to a maximum of Rs.10, 000 /- only.

sections.heading: Suggestions for Improvement
items: All crops and all the farmers should be brought under the purview of the scheme.
Premium rates should vary with the nature and indices of crop production in different areas.
The unit area considered for paying indemnity should be a village or group of villages as against block/mandal.
Threshold yield should be worked out on the basis of crop production indices over a ten year period as against five year period.

title: Principles of Cooperation
category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
definition: A set of principles of co-operation now followed worldwide, designed by the Rochdale pioneers.

sections.heading: The Important Principles of Co-Operation
items: 1. Principle of open and voluntary association: The admission and membership into a co-operative society is open to everybody irrespective of caste, religion, any social and political affiliations.
2. Principle of Democratic organization: Co-operatives are organized and managed based on the principle of democracy.
3. Principle of service: Co-operatives main aim is to cater to the needs of its members.
4. Principle of self-help and mutual help: The funds of society are contributed by the members in the form of share capital.
5. Principle of distribution of profits and surpluses: Co-operatives are not interested in making profits like business organizations.
6. Principle of political and religious neutrality: The important strength for growth of the cooperatives is the unity among the members and non-interference of political parties.
7. Principle of Education: If the members in cooperative society are illiterate, their participation is poor in running the cooperatives and they cannot understand what is going on in the society.
8. Principle of thrift: The cooperatives must aim at inculcating the habit of thrift i.e. ―propensity to save‖ among the members.
9. Principle of publicity: The cooperatives should make sincere efforts to tell their members about the society and all the dealings of the society should be made public.
10. Principle of honorary service: The honorary personnel will simply supervise and direct operations of cooperatives.

sections.heading: Maxims of Co-operation
items: 1. Better Farming: Helping the farmer to realize a better production in the farm business through adoption of requisite technology.
2. Better Business: Farmers should get a better deal in buying the inputs as well as disposing the products.
3. Better Living: The cooperative societies should supply consumer goods to the consumers at reasonable rates.

title: Advantages: The advantages that co-operative marketing can confer on the farmer are
category: Technical and Production Science
definition: Co-operative marketing can confer several advantages on farmers, including increased bargaining strength, direct dealing with final buyers, provision of credit, easier and cheaper transport, storage facilities, grading and standardization, market intelligence, influencing marketing prices, provision of inputs and consumer goods, and processing of agricultural produce.

sections.heading: Increases bargaining strength of the farmers
sections.content: Many of the defects of the present agricultural marketing system arise because often one ignorant and illiterate farmer has to face well-organised mass of clever intermediaries. If the farmers join hands and for a co-operative, naturally they will be less prone to exploitation and malpractices.

sections.heading: Direct dealing with final buyers
sections.content: The co-operatives can altogether skip the intermediaries and enter into direct relations with the final buyers. This practice will eliminate exploiters and ensure fair prices to both the producers and the consumers.

sections.heading: Provision of credit
sections.content: The marketing co-operative societies provide credit to the farmers to save them from the necessity of selling their produce immediately after harvesting. This ensures better returns to the farmers.

sections.heading: Easier and cheaper transport
sections.content: Bulk transport of agricultural produce by the societies is often easier and cheaper. Sometimes the societies have their own means of transport.

sections.heading: Storage facilities
sections.content: The co-operative marketing societies generally have storage facilities. Thus the farmers can wait for better prices.

sections.heading: Grading and standardization
sections.content: This task can be done more easily for a co-operative agency than for an individual farmer. For this purpose, they can seek assistance from the government or can even evolve their own grading arrangements.

sections.heading: Market intelligence
sections.content: The co-operatives can arrange to obtain data on market prices, demand and supply and other related information from the markets on a regular basis and can plan their activities accordingly.

sections.heading: Influencing marketing prices
sections.content: Wherever strong marketing co-operative are operative, they have bargained for and have achieved better prices for their agricultural produce.

sections.heading: Provision of inputs and consumer goods
sections.content: The co-operative marketing societies can easily arrange for bulk purchase of agricultural inputs, like seeds, manures fertilizers etc. and consumer goods at relatively lower price and can then distribute them to the members.

sections.heading: Processing of agricultural produce
sections.content: The co-operative societies can undertake processing activities like crushing seeds, ginning 'and pressing of cotton, etc.
